Demand Forecasting for Public Library Services
This paper examines how a four-site library
network can forecast demand for lending,
reference and programming services using
circulation logs, visitor counts and program
registrations. We treat forecasts as decision
aids rather than verdicts, and we separate
simulated observations from causal claims
throughout. The analysis covers data
preparation, model comparison, scenario
interpretation and the governance duties that
keep forecasts accountable to branch staff
and residents.
A Study Scope and
Forecasting Questions
The study addresses a practical question: how
many loans, visits and program seats should
each branch plan for in the coming cycle? We
frame forecasting as a planning instrument for
staffing, collection rotation and room booking,
not as a performance rating. The scope covers
the main circulating collections and public
programs across the participating sites, while
excluding interlibrary transfers and one-off
outreach events that follow their own
scheduling logic.
A.1 Data Sources and Preparation
Records come from circulation systems, door
counters and registration logs covering 2022
through 2025. We harmonize branch
identifiers, remove duplicate checkouts, and
flag closure days and system outages before
aggregation. Weekly series are constructed so
that holiday spikes are visible rather than
smoothed away, and every exclusion is logged
so that reviewers can reconstruct the
prepared dataset from the raw extracts.

Duplicate scans, staff test checkouts and bulk
class loans are removed under written rules
agreed with branch supervisors. Each removal
is tagged with a reason code, and a sample of
flagged rows is re-checked by a second
reviewer. The cleaning log records the rule
version applied, so a later analyst can
reproduce the same dataset and see exactly
which records changed and why.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
A.1.2 Handling Closures and
Seasonal Gaps
Closure days, renovation periods and holiday
weeks create gaps that distort naive
averages. We mark these intervals explicitly
and model them as known absences rather
than missing demand. Where a gap exceeds a
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
full week, the branch series is re-based on the
surrounding comparable weeks, and the
adjustment is documented alongside the
original counts so that planners can judge how
much of a forecast rests on imputed values.
A.2 Constructing Weekly Demand
Series
Weekly aggregates combine loans, visits and
program registrations into separate series
rather than a single composite index. Keeping
the series apart preserves interpretability: a
rise in visits without a matching rise in loans
suggests different service use. Each series
carries a data-quality flag, and weeks below a
completeness threshold are excluded from
model fitting but retained in the audit trail for
transparency.
B Model Comparison and
Validation
We compare a seasonal baseline, a regression
with calendar and weather covariates, and a
gradient-boosted model across the prepared
series. Validation uses rolling-origin splits so
that each model is tested only on weeks after
its training window. Accuracy is reported per
branch and per service line, because
aggregate scores can hide a branch where a
model consistently under-predicts weekend
demand.
B.1 Evaluation Metrics and Error
Patterns
Forecast error is summarized with mean
absolute percentage error and a bias measure
that reveals systematic over- or
under-prediction. Errors cluster around school
holiday transitions and program launch weeks,
which suggests calendar features deserve
more weight than weather variables. We also
report error by branch size, since small
branches show wider relative error even when
absolute differences are modest.
Supporting records are presented in Table 4.
B.1.1 Backtesting Across Branches
Backtests replay 12 weeks of history for each
of the 4 sites, refitting models at fixed
intervals. Results show that the seasonal
baseline is competitive for loans but weaker
for program registrations, which respond to
announcement timing. These are simulated
backtest observations, not evidence that any
single model causes better service outcomes;
they indicate where model choice matters
most for planning.
Figure 2: Interpretation guide for forecast intervals by
service
B.1.2 Interpreting Forecast
Intervals
Point forecasts are presented with prediction
intervals so planners can see the plausible
range. A branch planning staffing against the
upper bound will over-staff on average, while
planning against the lower bound risks queues
at peak hours. We recommend choosing the
interval width according to the cost of being
wrong for each service, and we label intervals
as simulated estimates rather than
guarantees.

B.2 Governance and
Implementation Duties
Forecasts enter branch planning only after a
review meeting where supervisors check
assumptions, note local events and record
dissent. The review produces a decision memo
with owners and review dates, and model
changes require a documented rationale. This
governance keeps forecasting accountable:
staff know which numbers drive rosters, and
residents can ask how service levels were set
without confronting an unexplained algorithm.

forecasts drive rosters
Branch supervisors should confirm that
holiday calendars used in fitting match the
actual closure schedule; a mismatch quietly
shifts seasonal effects and inflates error in the
weeks surrounding each break.
When a counter fails for part of a day, the
affected week should be flagged rather than
scaled up, because scaling assumes a stable
visitor pattern that the outage itself may have
disturbed.
Model documentation should name the
training window, feature set and validation
split so that a later analyst can reproduce
results without reconstructing decisions from
memory or informal notes.
Program registration series often lead actual
attendance; planners should keep both
measures visible so that forecasted demand
reflects seats offered as well as seats filled.
Rolling-origin validation is preferred to a single
holdout because library demand shifts
gradually and one split can flatter a model
that performs poorly in other periods.
Where two models disagree sharply for a
branch, the review meeting should record
both ranges and the reasoning behind the
chosen planning figure rather than averaging
silently.
Small branches need wider intervals; treating
their forecasts with the same precision as
large sites invites overconfidence in staffing
and collection decisions.
Weather covariates add little explanatory
value in our simulated tests, so teams should
weigh whether the data collection burden is
justified before retaining them.
Renovation periods should be excluded from
fitting but retained in reporting, since planners
still need to know what demand looked like
before and after the disruption.
Forecast review should occur before roster
deadlines, not after, so that adjustments can
still influence staffing rather than merely
annotate past choices.
Any change to cleaning rules should trigger a
refit and a short note explaining the expected
effect, because rule changes can move error
metrics without any real change in demand.
Reference desk queries are poorly captured by

door counters alone; a separate tally or
sampling scheme improves visibility into
demand that never reaches the circulation
system.
